item.title: Outdated Home Devices Pose Major Network Security Risks
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: The oldest gadget in your house could be your home network's biggest security hole
Outdated home devices pose significant security risks. The FBI warned in 2025 that end-of-life (EOL) routers, often from 2010 or earlier, are targeted by malware like TheMoon, which exploits open ports and vulnerable scripts to install proxies for criminal anonymity. A 2024 Consumer Reports study found most smart appliance brands do not disclose update durations, with only three of 19 major brands offering support beyond five years. Cisco reported that 40% of exploited vulnerabilities in 2025 targeted EOL devices, many over a decade old. Routers and cameras, if unpatched, can be recruited into botnets to attack websites. Consumers are advised to audit connected devices, check for firmware updates, and replace EOL hardware. WPA3 security standards are recommended, with WPA2/WPA3 compatibility for older gadgets. Separating outdated devices into a separate network can limit damage if compromised.

item.title: KAIST AI reads lips in silence with 19.4% error rate
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Original headline: Scientists taught AI to read lips in total silence, and the results are pretty impressive
KAIST researchers developed an AI system called DLLM-VSR that translates lip movements into text without audio. The system achieved a 19.4% word error rate on the LRS3 benchmark using 433 hours of labeled video data. Unlike traditional sequential processing, the AI identifies confident parts of a sentence first, then uses contextual clues to fill in gaps. It estimates multiple sentence lengths and selects the most plausible result. Potential applications include accessibility tools for the deaf and industrial communication in noisy environments. However, the technology isn't ready for real-time use due to computational demands and dataset variability. Privacy concerns arise from its ability to interpret conversations from silent video recordings. The research highlights AI's potential to enhance communication in challenging acoustic conditions.

item.title: Nvidia Prepares Backup Plan for China's Self-Driving Industry
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: TechCrunch Mobility: The Nvidia backup plan for China’s self-driving industry
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair, raising concerns about U.S.-China tech relations. Chinese autonomous vehicle companies face challenges due to potential export restrictions on Nvidia chips. Leo Wang, CFO of Pony.ai, noted demand for Nvidia chips exceeds supply, prompting the company to adopt domestic alternatives. 'Domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,' Wang said, emphasizing existing alternatives despite higher costs. Companies like Pony.ai are preparing 'Plan B' strategies, with Wang stating, 'Everyone... is practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years.' Meanwhile, other mobility updates include May Mobility's 10,000 autonomous vehicle target, Newmo's $135 million funding, and Waymo's software recall under investigation by the NHTSA.

item.title: Plural Raises $1.1B for Europe’s Early-Stage Moonshot Investments
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Helsing backer Plural raises $1.1B to fund Europe’s next moonshots
Plural, a European venture capital firm, raised €1 billion ($1.1 billion) to fund early-stage and follow-on investments. Two-thirds of the capital will go to its third early-stage fund, while one-third supports a new 'opportunities' fund targeting select follow-on investments. Partners Khaled Helioui and Carina Namih emphasized Plural’s commitment to early-stage ventures, including 'moonshot' projects like Proxima Fusion and The Exploration Company. The fund will focus on energy, AI infrastructure, defense, health, and other capital-intensive sectors. Helioui noted European entrepreneurs, particularly second-time founders, are increasingly prioritizing projects that enhance national sovereignty and resilience. Plural’s Tallinn office played a key role in defense investments, including Hypersonica, a missile company. The firm expanded its presence with offices in London and Paris, hiring Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty in October 2025. Partners will lead small investment portfolios, offering support ranging from hiring to finance. The shift reflects growing alignment between European and U.S. venture capital models.

item.title: 3D Printing Tool Enables Non-Planar Printing Across All Axes
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: 3D printing dev’s free tool unlocks curved printing along all three axes
Alpaca Engineering's PancakeSlicer enables non-planar 3D printing across all three axes by simplifying complex slicing workflows. The tool addresses the challenge of non-planar printing, which requires precise collision avoidance during multi-axis movement. By using 3D models of print heads from supported printers like Bambu Lab, Prusa, and Creality, PancakeSlicer calculates safe print paths. It offers self-hosting via desktop, NAS, or home server with a web UI, allowing multiple users to manage print jobs remotely. The slicer also unifies printer management across brands, replacing multiple slicer apps for multi-printer setups. Unlike previous attempts, PancakeSlicer integrates 3D printer management features into its workflow, making non-planar printing accessible without manual G-code input. The project aims to encourage broader experimentation and practical adoption of non-planar techniques, which are currently limited to research due to complexity and lack of user-friendly tools.

item.title: Gallery showcases 357 CPU die shots from 1971 to 2024
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: 357 detailed CPU die shots spanning 1971 to 2024 crammed into a new gallery
A gallery hosts 357 detailed CPU die shots from 1971 to 2024, curated by an unnamed collator. The collection, available at sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies, includes images from Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz. Users can browse in gallery, true scale, or table views, with filters for processor maker, year, die dimensions, and licensing. The site allows searching for specific CPUs, such as 17 variants of the 486 architecture. Notable entries include the Motorola 68000 and AMD Athlon XP. Some eras, like Intel's Ivy Bridge and Haswell generations, are underrepresented. The collator suggests adding details like die area and transistor count for improvement. Users can click thumbnails for larger views or open images in new tabs for full detail. The site lacks recent contributions and some metadata fields.

item.title: Moth Quantum Sets Quantum Data Retrieval Record with IBM Hardware
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: A major breakthrough has claimed to set a world record for encoding data onto a quantum computer — and, crucially, reading it back again
Moth Quantum claims a quantum computing breakthrough by storing and retrieving 1,568 numerical values on IBM’s 120-qubit Phoenix processor. The Tessa technique uses neighboring qubits to store data, avoiding long-distance transfers and reducing operations. It recreated images from stored values, achieving a 0.69 correlation with the source for a color image, compared to 0.95–0.96 for simpler images. Average numerical errors were 0.130 on Phoenix and 0.131 on Fez, improving to 0.075–0.078 after adjustments using known data. Tests with audio, DNA, and proteins showed varying accuracy: 49.3% for music notes, 71.5% for p53 protein, and 92.3% for MT-CO3. However, errors remained high for complex sequences, with Phoenix’s brightness error exceeding predicted noise levels. The study warns that current hardware lacks error correction and full interference modeling, limiting medical applications. Moth Quantum’s Daniel Bultrini noted Tessa optimizes chip capabilities, while founder Harry Kumar emphasized its importance for AI-driven quantum applications.
item.source: Latest from TechRadar US in News

item.title: Developer bypasses Coway air purifier's cloud with local control hack
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Dev hacks Coway air purifier to cut it off from the cloud
Developer Scott J. Goldman bypassed Coway's cloud system for his Airmega IconS air purifier by exploiting a security flaw. The purifier downloads a root certificate over unencrypted HTTP, which Goldman intercepted and replaced using mitmproxy and nftables. This allowed his Home Assistant server to act as a local intermediary, bypassing Coway's IoCare cloud. The cloud integration was unreliable, with frequent outages and server downtime, and his account was banned for using an outdated integration. AI tools helped automate parts of the setup, including firewall rules and Bluetooth protocol reconstruction. The result is local control via Home Assistant and Apple Home, though the setup is experimental and lacks features like air-quality metrics and firmware updates. The project, called coway-local, requires HA Core 2026.10.2 and 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, disconnecting the purifier from Coway's cloud. Goldman aims to avoid reliance on Coway's potential future service fees or discontinued cloud services.

item.title: Indian startup Bharat Semi raises $24M for AI image sensors
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors. The startup, based in New Delhi, has secured design wins with U.S. defense firm General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its sensors combine image capture, processing, and AI on a single chip, potentially reducing system costs by 70% compared to traditional setups. Co-founder Vrinda Kapoor said the technology targets markets like smart homes, industrial automation, and aerospace. The all-equity round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital and others. Bharat Semi plans to expand its U.S. team to 20 by mid-2027 and hire engineers in Europe. The startup aims to launch first-generation sensors in prototype form and second-generation models by mid-2027. It also announced a separate semiconductor fabrication project with the U.S. Space Force, though it will remain fabless, outsourcing manufacturing while focusing on design and software.

item.title: Sony Patents PlayStation Controller with Card Reader for Payments
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: A Card Reader Could Be Coming to PlayStation Controllers. Maybe.
Sony has filed a patent for a PlayStation controller that could include a card or NFC/RFID reader to streamline payment processes. The patent, spotted by Engadget, aims to address issues with performing multiple operations on the console, such as entering payment details or login information, which can slow down performance. The proposed feature would allow the controller to receive payment data from a nearby phone or card and transmit it to the console, potentially improving user experience. While the patent is vague, it suggests a hybrid card reader could be added to the controller, enabling convenient interactions between devices, like logging into accounts from a friend’s phone. The move comes as physical PlayStation games are set to phase out by January 2028, pushing digital purchases to the forefront.

item.title: Sudden Phone Battery Drops Linked to Aging Batteries and Software Updates
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?
Sudden phone battery drops can result from aging lithium-ion batteries or recent software updates. Phones estimate battery levels based on voltage and current, which can lead to abrupt percentage drops when the battery's actual charge differs from the estimate. Older batteries lose capacity and may fail during power-intensive tasks, causing the phone to misread remaining charge. Software updates and background apps also contribute to increased battery consumption. High temperatures exacerbate battery drain, and phones are rated for operation between 0° and 35° C. Post-update battery spikes are temporary as systems optimize files. Users should close background apps, limit location access, and check battery settings to identify drains. Battery diagnostics tools in Pixel 6 and later, Samsung Galaxy, and iPhones provide health details. Apple claims newer iPhones retain 80% capacity after 1,000 charge cycles, suggesting replacement if below this threshold.

item.title: Apple's Smart Glasses Launch in 2027 with Siri and Design Focus
item.description:
Source: The Verge, Digital Trends Original headline: Apple's First Smart Glasses Set for 2027 Launch with Focus on Design and Siri Integration
Apple is preparing to launch its first smart glasses in 2027, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The device will lack augmented reality features, focusing instead on Siri-powered interactions, enhanced audio quality, and a design that blends with traditional eyewear. Shipment could begin before year-end 2027, though a full launch date remains unconfirmed. The project, codenamed N50, uses a pared-down version of visionOS and a new processor based on Apple’s smartwatch chip architecture. Design details suggest a sleek, thin profile similar to Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, with embedded cameras in oval openings for visual recognition. A flat, rectangular MagSafe-like charger enables wireless charging without removing the glasses. Software integration relies on Siri for voice-controlled app interactions, with iOS 27.3 introducing precise voice commands. Features like Visual Intelligence, real-time translation, and smart home controls will be included, though third-party apps will run on paired iPhones. Apple emphasizes privacy and audio quality, with no Android support planned. The 2027 timeline reflects a cautious approach to refining the product before broader release.

item.title: AO3 is back online but with limited features
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Archive of Our Own (AO3) is back online after a two-week outage caused by a security incident. The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), which runs AO3, temporarily disabled features like icons and external work importing, and limited downloads to HTML format. Full functionality is expected to resume soon. OTW confirmed the incident did not involve data deletion, with user works, bookmarks, and drafts remaining intact. Drafts deleted during downtime will be removed starting November 29. Users are advised to check drafts and update passwords due to potential security risks. OTW partnered with a security firm to review the incident but will not disclose specifics. The organization emphasized no user database compromise was confirmed, though users are urged to change passwords and update linked accounts.

item.title: KTC to Present 31.5-Inch 6K Mini-LED Monitor at CES 2027
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: KTC heads to CES 2027 with a 31.5-inch 6K Mini-LED display engineered to break records
KTC is preparing a 31.5-inch 6K Mini-LED monitor for CES 2027. The M32P2 model features 6,016 x 3,384 resolution at 60Hz, 2,304 local dimming zones, and peak brightness of 1,000 nits for HDR content. It includes 98% Adobe RGB, 99% DCI-P3, and 100% sRGB color coverage. Connectivity options include HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, USB-C, and three USB 3.0 ports. The display supports 1.07 billion colors via 8-bit plus FRC and has a 1,000:1 contrast ratio. KTC’s pricing history suggests affordability, with previous 5K and Mini-LED models selling for under $530 and $300 respectively. A marketing specialist noted the CES units are unfinished samples, not yet launched. Final pricing remains undisclosed, though KTC’s approach to advanced technology at accessible prices could make this display competitive in professional markets.
item.source: Latest from TechRadar US in News

item.title: INSTRUCTION: iOS 27 Adds Six Non-AI Features for Older iPhones
item.description:
Source: PCMag Original headline: Have an Older iPhone? Here Are 6 Handy iOS 27 Features That Don't Require AI
iOS 27 introduces six non-AI features for older iPhones. Liquid Glass customization allows precise control via a slider in Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass. The Camera app lets users pin favorite controls to the top of the screen for quick access. A new feature lets users save individual video frames as photos within the Photos app. Enhanced slideshow options include customizable transitions, duration settings, and music adjustments. These updates are available to any iPhone that can be upgraded to iOS 27, regardless of whether it supports Apple Intelligence. The changes focus on improving user experience without requiring AI capabilities. Users can adjust Liquid Glass transparency, streamline camera controls, and refine photo and video editing tools. The updates emphasize accessibility and efficiency for older devices.

item.title: Apple Studies User Interaction with Health AI Tools
item.description:
Source: Engadget, The Verge, TechCrunch, Digital Trends Original headline: Apple Launches Health AI Study to Improve User Experience and Trust
Apple has launched a research study to examine user interaction with AI-powered health tools, aiming to enhance their effectiveness and usability. The Apple Health AI Usage Study, in partnership with OpenEvidence, features an app allowing participants to ask health questions and rate responses for accuracy, detail, and relevance. The app is available in the U.S. for iPhone 15 Pro users running iOS 26, with enrollment open to adults aged 21 and older. Apple plans to recruit up to 200,000 participants over 12 months. Users can share Apple HealthKit data, including activity, sleep, and lab results, but all data will be anonymized and not used to train AI models. OpenEvidence deletes query and response data after 24 hours. Responses are based on peer-reviewed medical sources like The New England Journal of Medicine. Monthly surveys will gather feedback, and the app aims to help users prepare for doctor visits. Apple’s vice president, Sumbul Desai, MD, emphasized scientific rigor in health AI. The app does not integrate with Siri or Apple Intelligence, relying on dictation instead. Apple clarified the study is not focused on releasing new Health app features but may explore future integration. The initiative follows rising interest in health AI, with OpenAI reporting over 300 million weekly health queries. The study’s findings could shape broader health AI development, as noted by UCSF’s Dr. Robert Wachter, who highlighted potential improvements in patient-doctor interactions.
item.source: Engadget, The Verge, TechCrunch, Digital Trends

item.title: Enthusiast builds working 486 DX2 PC on breadboard in 16 days
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Enthusiast builds a working 486 DX2 retro PC on a breadboard in just 16 days, immediately runs Doom
An app engineer based in Tokyo built a working 486 DX2 PC on a breadboard in 16 days, running Doom. The project began on October 24 with the acquisition of a DX2 66 MHz Intel CPU, followed by a Colorlight i9 v7.2 FPGA board for chipset duties. By October 26, the system’s form took shape, and the CPU blinked an LED using x86 code. RAM was added on October 31, microSD storage on November 3, and FreeDOS 1.3 booted successfully. A custom CRT-style monitor, 3D-printed with a Raspberry Pi panel, was completed alongside the system. On November 9, the breadboard PC and monitor were showcased, with Doom running smoothly on the 1992-era hardware. The enthusiast plans to refine the project for full PC-98 compatibility. A similar breadboard-based 386 system was previously reported in April.

item.title: University of Rochester Modifies Ender 3 into $450 Bioprinter for Engineered Living Materials
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Modified Ender 3 becomes a $450 bioprinter for 3D printing engineered living materials
Microbiologists at the University of Rochester modified an Ender 3 FDM 3D printer into a $450 bioprinter for engineered living materials (ELM) research. The team adapted standard 3D printing workflows using SolidWorks and Slic3r, adjusting settings for a custom syringe pump print head. The bioprinter uses a 10 mL glass Luer-lock syringe with a plunger mechanism to extrude bio-ink composed of bacteria and alginate. Support slurry, made from agarose or gelatin enriched with calcium ions, stabilizes the printed structures, allowing ELMs to remain viable for four or more weeks. The researchers designed custom PETG components for the syringe pump and optimized print settings for a 0.254mm needle, achieving a 2 mL/h flow rate. ELMs, which include bacteria-based materials, could enable applications like antimicrobial treatments, plastic degradation, wastewater treatment, and biodegradable plastics. The open-source, affordable bioprinter aims to accelerate ELM research by reducing hardware costs and improving accessibility.

item.title: Intel reclaims overall CPU market share for the first time since 2025
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Intel regained overall x86 CPU market share from AMD for the first time since Q2 2025, driven by strong desktop PC performance. Mercury Research reports Q3 2026 x86 CPU shipments declined 10% sequentially and 12% year-over-year, with client processor demand weakening due to rising component costs. Server CPU shipments grew 20% YoY to 8.13 million units, fueled by AI infrastructure growth. AMD maintained dominance in mobile and server segments, with 29.2% mobile CPU share and 35.5% server share. Intel's desktop CPU share rose to 70.1%, up from 65.4% in Q3 2025, while AMD's client share fell to 29.3%. Analysts note PC demand softened in Q3, with OEMs reducing inventories and DIY channels remaining weak. Both companies expect client CPU shipments to drop over 20% in Q4. AMD's mobile share increased 0.3% to 29.2%, its highest ever, while Intel's server share fell to 64.5% from 72.3% a year earlier. Component price pressures, particularly memory and 3D NAND, continue to weigh on PC demand.

item.title: Why your Wi-Fi slows down when more devices connect
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Wi-Fi slows when more devices connect due to bandwidth limits and congestion. Routers function like train stations, managing traffic between devices and the internet. Modern homes have far more connected gadgets than in the past, straining older Wi-Fi standards. Wi-Fi 6 and 6E routers handle up to 9.6Gbps, while Wi-Fi 7 reaches 46Gbps, but local device communication also uses bandwidth. Band congestion occurs as 2.4GHz has only three non-overlapping channels, easily overwhelmed by low-power devices. Routers have limits on simultaneous connections, with Wi-Fi 5 handling only 10-25 devices. Upgrading to Wi-Fi 7 helps but requires compatible devices. Using 5GHz or 6GHz bands reduces congestion, though mesh routers lack this option. Pausing non-essential devices during heavy usage and switching to hub-based smart home systems can alleviate strain. Standalone Wi-Fi bulbs compete for channels, while hubs use protocols like Thread or Zigbee with minimal Wi-Fi demand.

item.title: Kongsberg Converts Fishing Vessels into Autonomous Submarine Hunters for Royal Navy
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: Shipping giant wants to convert a fishing trawler into a 200-ft unmanned Arctic Russian submarine hunter for the British Royal Navy
Norwegian maritime engineering firm Kongsberg Maritime proposes converting commercial fishing trawlers into autonomous submarine hunters for the British Royal Navy. The Arctic Hunter concept involves 56-meter vessels equipped with Thales UK sonar systems and secure communications technology, designed to operate independently for 60 days without a crew. Modifications include noise-reducing propulsion systems to enhance acoustic monitoring. The design aligns with Britain's Type 92 program, aiming for affordable autonomous vessels to assist conventional warships in anti-submarine warfare. Inspired by WWII-era conversions of whaling ships into naval escorts, the plan envisions 10 vessels operating near Bear Gap, a strategic passage between Norway and Svalbard. Kongsberg emphasizes using existing commercial ship designs to reduce military construction costs, though no official contract has been awarded. The vessels would complement future Type 26 frigates being built for UK, Australia, Canada, and Norway, supporting a hybrid naval fleet strategy.
item.source: Latest from TechRadar US in News

item.title: Jensen Huang's Resignation Sparks Concerns Over AI Industry Stability
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Original headline: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after allegations of affairs with executives linked to Chinese intelligence. The board launched an investigation, with CFO Collette Kress serving as interim CEO. Rebecca Bellan noted Huang's central role in Nvidia's success, stating 'so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.' National security concerns arose due to Huang's advocacy for loosening chip exports to China, which could aid Chinese AI development. Analysts questioned trust in his leadership amid these conflicts. Huang's resignation accelerated after a Bloomberg report suggested Nvidia's attorney had probed Alice Huang's ties to Chinese intelligence. The incident raised questions about Nvidia's influence over the AI industry, given its 80% market share in AI GPUs and $99 billion in investments in startups like OpenAI and Anthropic. The board's response highlighted risks to Nvidia's strategic position in the AI ecosystem.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to Clear Application Cache on Mac
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: How to clear the application cache on your Mac
Mac applications store temporary files called caches to improve performance. These caches can consume storage space over time. Users can manually clear app caches by accessing the ~/library/caches folder, which contains cached data for both Apple and third-party apps. First-party Apple apps use 'com.apple' in their identifiers, while third-party apps do not. Caches may also reside in ~/library/containers for sandboxed apps. Clearing caches can free storage space or resolve glitches but may temporarily slow app performance as the cache rebuilds. Apps typically rely on caches for smooth operation, so users should only clear them if storage is constrained or if issues arise. Deleting caches does not inherently improve performance unless storage is limited.

item.title: DC Council Votes on Online Casino Bill Before Dec. 15 Deadline
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Original headline: DC online casino and sweepstakes ban bill gets Nov. 18 committee vote before Dec. 15 cutoff
The DC Council’s Committee on Human Services will vote on B26-0656, a bill legalizing online casinos and banning dual-currency sweepstakes casinos, on Nov. 18. The bill, first heard in May, requires regulatory certification before launch and includes enforcement tools like cease-and-desist letters and potential court action. The Office of Lottery and Gaming, which would regulate the market, supports the measure. Licensing terms favor existing operators, with $50,000 application fees and no license caps. Sportsbook licensees like BetMGM and Caesars could get expedited reviews. The bill’s passage would allow DC to join jurisdictions with legal online casinos. Amendments during the markup will determine if proposed changes by Office of Lottery and Gaming director Thomas R. Burnside are included. The bill must pass by Dec. 15 to avoid lapsing at the end of Council Period 26.

item.title: Disney Wants You to Know ‘VisionQuest’ Ended As a Success
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
Disney+ show 'VisionQuest' concluded with its finale, 'Forever,' reaching 3.7 million views in one day, the highest viewership for any Disney+ Marvel show since Loki's second season in 2023. The finale's viewership increased 44% compared to the previous episode, with overall viewership rising steadily throughout the show's five-week run. The finale also spurred a spike in ticket sales for 'Avengers: Doomsday,' though exact figures were not disclosed. The episode resolved Wanda Maximoff's storyline, with her surviving a 'death by mountain' reference from 'Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,' a plot point previously mocked by Ultron. Fans celebrated her return, though her future remains uncertain. Disney highlighted the success of Marvel's Wanda/Vision trilogy, which has been popular since its debut five years ago, suggesting potential future appearances in films or TV.

item.title: Samsung Discontinues AR Apps in December
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Samsung is discontinuing these useful mobile apps in December
Samsung is removing Quick Measure and AR Doodle from the Galaxy Store on December 31. The apps, which offer augmented reality tools for measuring objects and sketching with 3D effects, will no longer accept new downloads or updates after that date. Existing users can continue using the apps but may face functionality issues or compatibility problems with future OS updates beyond 2027. Samsung warned that some features might stop working properly without updates. The company apologized for the inconvenience and mentioned it may reintroduce the apps or their features in the future, though no timeline was provided. Users are encouraged to download the apps before the deadline to avoid losing access.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Tips to Prevent Overnight 3D Print Failures
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: 4 ways to fail-proof your long overnight 3D prints
3D printing overnight can lead to failures like filament jams or power interruptions. To reduce risks, ensure printer calibration is accurate to prevent errors during long prints. Address first-layer adhesion issues with brims, adjusted bed temperatures, or hairspray. Use a portable power station like Ecoflow to maintain power during blackouts or brief outages, as printers may not resume after full bed cooling. Check filament spool weight before starting to avoid run-out sensor pauses, and subtract empty spool weight for accuracy. Multi-material printers should be set to load identical filament automatically. Test complex prints on smaller scales first to catch design flaws. Some printers offer AI-based failure detection via cameras or plugins like OctoPrint to monitor prints remotely. No method guarantees success, but these steps improve reliability for overnight jobs.

item.title: Hacker Runs Doom on USB Drive's LCD Using AI Reverse-Engineering
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Hacker gets Doom running on a USB flash drive's built-in LCD, played by copying files
Hardware hacker Aaron Christophel ran Doom on a USB flash drive's built-in LCD by reverse-engineering its hardware. Using AI, he extracted firmware from the MOVESPEED MSSU10 drive, which has a 128GB capacity and costs about 50 euros. The drive's display chip, marked with SanDisk components, was modified by removing its identifier and accessing a debug port. A script called doomctl.py translated keyboard inputs into file transfers to control the game, mapping arrow keys to movement and spacebar to firing. Performance was limited to 13 frames per second, though game logic ran at Doom's normal 35 ticks per second. The project, open-sourced with code and firmware, highlights the drive's 200 MHz clock discrepancy, which measured 40.2 MHz. The drive lacks sound hardware, and only the first Doom map fits in its flash. Christophel noted AI enabled the hack, which could inspire similar modifications.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Spotting Fake SD Cards Is Easier Than You Think
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: Spotting a fake SD card is easier than you think
Fake SD cards have plagued consumers for years, with prices doubling since 2025 due to chip shortages. Experts warn that counterfeit cards can cause data loss or corruption, often appearing cheaper than genuine ones. Warning signs include suspiciously low prices, unverified sellers like Amazon or eBay, and missing packaging details. Testing tools like H2testw, f3, and CrystalDiskMark can verify a card's capacity and performance. H2testw checks storage and speed, while f3 uses pseudorandom data to detect fraud. CrystalDiskMark compares read/write speeds to packaging claims. Consumers are advised to buy from physical retailers or check warranty information to avoid counterfeit risks. Testing before use is recommended to prevent file loss.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: iPhone Notes app offers 10 advanced features beyond basic note-taking
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: 10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes
Apple's Notes app offers advanced features beyond basic note-taking. Math Notes allows equations to be solved and graphs plotted in real time, with automatic updates for variables. The app can scan documents, crop, and straighten pages, supporting digital signatures. Audio recordings of lectures or meetings are transcribed and searchable, with summaries available on newer iPhones. Image Wand transforms rough sketches into polished images using AI, with photorealistic results in iOS 27. Shared notes enable real-time collaboration for family or work projects. Apple Intelligence tools can proofread, reformat, and summarize text, converting notes into tables or bullet points. iOS 27 adds divider lines, color highlights, and section links for better organization. The reed pen in Markup tools mimics traditional calligraphy. Some features require newer iPhones (15 Pro, 16 models) or iOS 27 for full functionality. Scans are saved as PDFs, and AI-generated images carry a SynthID watermark. These tools enhance productivity for students, professionals, and everyday users.

item.title: Pentagon Tests Autonomous War Robots in Combat Simulations
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Pentagon tests pack hunting with autonomous war robots
The Pentagon tested autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat at Fort Knox’s St. Vith Range in October. Four UGVs operated as a team, using drones and satellite data to surveil and identify targets under human control. The exercise, part of DARPA’s RACER program, demonstrated modular UGVs capable of carrying payloads like drones, rockets, and sensors. A scout UGV led the pack, using a drone for aerial reconnaissance, while others provided cover. Human operators directed kinetic actions, with all movement and detection handled autonomously. The test aimed to enhance battlefield capabilities for European allies, reflecting real-world terrain. UGVs can now navigate off-road at human speeds and are ready for logistics and combat roles. Further tests with soldiers are planned for December.

item.title: Free 3D Printer Filament Drying Method Uses Existing Box and Printer
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: You can dry your 3D printer filament for free, just don't throw away the box it came in
3D printer filament can absorb moisture, causing print failures. A free drying method uses the original filament box and a printer's heated bed. Cut the box's lid, poke ventilation holes, and place the spool on the heated bed. Hot air circulates through the box, evaporating moisture. A heated bed set to 70C or higher is required, as cold-bed printers cannot use this method. A YouTuber's test showed this DIY approach outperformed several commercial dryers. After drying, store filament in airtight containers with desiccants to prevent future moisture absorption. Users must perform the process safely, monitoring for signs of overheating. The method avoids purchasing a dedicated dryer but requires proper storage to maintain filament quality.

item.title: ULA Vulcan Rocket Failure Destroys 40 Amazon Satellites
item.description:
Source: The Verge, Engadget Original headline: ULA Vulcan Rocket Failure Destroys 40 Amazon Leo Satellites, Marks First Mission Failure in 20 Years
United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket failed during a launch, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites. The anomaly occurred 10 minutes into the flight, preventing the payload from reaching orbit. This marks ULA's first mission failure in two decades. Amazon expressed confidence in ULA, noting risks are inherent to inaugural missions. The Vulcan, a newer heavy-lift vehicle, faced technical challenges including a hold 20 seconds before liftoff. The launch, delayed due to refueling issues, saw the first-stage methane engines fire longer than expected. The hydrogen-powered Centaur upper stage's 12.25-minute burn encountered an anomaly. The failure impacts Amazon's Leo project, which requires 38 Vulcan launches to deploy its satellite constellation. With only 390 satellites currently in orbit, the setback delays the project's timeline. Amazon had already faced delays from Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket explosion. ULA acknowledged scheduling slips affecting satellite initiatives. The incident highlights challenges in deploying large satellite networks and the importance of reliable launch systems.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: 1000Wh Power Station Runtime Depends on Device Power and Efficiency
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: How long can a 1000 watt-hour power station run your devices?
A 1000 watt-hour power station's runtime depends on device power consumption, conversion efficiency, and usage patterns. A 1,024Wh unit like the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 can theoretically power a 200W fridge for over five hours or a 65W laptop for 15+ hours. In practice, Jackery only guarantees four hours for the fridge and 11 hours for the laptop due to energy conversion losses. AC outlets convert DC power, wasting 5-20% efficiency, and plugging in adapters like phone chargers adds further inefficiency. Device power usage varies widely—gaming laptops can consume over 200W under load, while phones fluctuate based on activity. To maximize runtime, use built-in USB ports for mobile devices, avoid extreme temperatures (optimal 59-95F/15-35C), and minimize full charge cycles to preserve battery capacity. Portable power stations degrade over time, reducing usable capacity with each recharge cycle.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Apple's Switch Control lets users control multiple devices
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: You can control your other devices with this resourceful Apple feature
Apple's Switch Control allows users to control multiple devices on the same Wi-Fi network using alternate input methods. The feature, part of iOS's accessibility tools, lets users set up external controllers, gestures, or head movements to operate devices. To enable, users must connect devices to the same Wi-Fi and iCloud account, then activate Switch Control on each device. The 'Use Other Devices for Switch Control' option lets users select compatible devices from a network list and assign existing switches to control them. Non-Apple controllers, including game pads and Bluetooth keyboards, can also be used. While designed for accessibility, users have found ways to automate tasks in apps like Kindle or games. The feature requires pairing devices and configuring switches through the Settings app, with options to stop control sessions. Apple emphasizes its role in aiding mobility, but its versatility extends beyond basic accessibility uses.

item.title: Lenovo’s detachable Googlebook Duet 13 leaks with January launch
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Original headline: Lenovo’s first detachable Googlebook just leaked, and it could launch in January
Lenovo’s first detachable Googlebook, the Duet 13, has leaked with a January launch date. Leaker Evan Blass shared renders showing a 13-inch tablet with a detachable keyboard featuring curved keys, a small trackpad, and a 'Googlebook' label. The design includes a back cover that folds into a stand with prominent Lenovo branding, a Glowbar next to rear cameras, and potential USB-C ports. Specs suggest 16GB RAM and a MediaTek Dimensity CX C10 Max chip, though price and storage remain unknown. The device aims to be the first detachable Googlebook, differing from current laptops and foldable models like Acer’s Googlebook14. Software limitations exist, with interface elements only functioning in landscape mode. Google confirmed detachables are in development, but Lenovo must justify the detachable design over existing options. The device is expected to debut at CES 2027, though neither Lenovo nor Google has officially confirmed details.

item.title: Anthropic Indicates Recursive Self-Improvement Threshold May Be Met
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Original headline: Anthropic Says Its Recursive Self-Improvement Alarm Has Been Triggered
Anthropic disclosed in its November 2 S-1 filing that its AI technology may have crossed a threshold requiring precautions related to recursive self-improvement. The company later revised its November 10 version of the document, removing explicit references to 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI' but indicating the Responsible Scaling Policy's relevant section has activated. The threshold is based on expected future model performance and overall progress rates, not current observations. Mitigations now include enhancing security, achieving 'eyes on everything' oversight, and advanced red teaming. Anthropic's IPO is imminent, with shares set to trade publicly. Founders' letters in the IPO documents emphasize the need to modulate AI capability growth, particularly when driven by self-improving systems. The company cites internal estimates suggesting further acceleration in AI capabilities.

item.title: Composers Explain How 007 First Light Score Balances Narrative and Player Experience
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Original headline: 'Sometimes we are simply scene setting, other times we are helping shape the emotional moments, or enforcing the action' — 007 First Light composers explain how they scored the game to serve both the narrative and the player
Composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith for 007 First Light joined the project 18 months before release, working with advanced footage to align the score with the game's vision. They emphasized balancing narrative and player experience, using cinematic sections for storytelling while guiding gameplay through music. Smith noted the game's 'cinematic' style allowed traditional scoring in some parts but required music to inform player actions in others. Henson highlighted the dual role of composing for both the game and the player, stressing the need for music to enhance immersion without disrupting it. The soundtrack is nominated for Best Original Video Game Score at the Ivors Composer Awards on November 17, 2026. Both composers praised IO Interactive's openness to collaboration, describing their integration into the audio team and the creative freedom afforded to them.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Free Android app reads USB-C cable specs in seconds
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Original headline: Can't tell your USB-C cable's specs? This free Android app reads them in seconds
USB-C cables appear identical but vary in specifications like power ratings and charging protocols. A free Android app, USB-C Tester: Cable & Charger, reads these details instantly. The app provides real-time data on voltage, amperage, wattage, and charging standards such as Qualcomm Quick Charge and Samsung/Apple fast charging. It also detects e-marker chips, Power Delivery, and PPS protocols. Users can save logs, export diagnostic reports in CSV/PDF, and set alerts for overheating or voltage issues. The app requires Android 9+ and is 5MB, with updates as recent as November 4, 2026. Similar tools exist for iOS and desktop platforms, including WattCheck, WhatCable, and USB Device Tree Viewer.

item.title: 13-Year-Old Inventor Creates Low-Cost Solar Panel Tracker
item.description:
Source: Engadget Original headline: How one 13-year-old is helping solve a huge solar panel limitation
Jason Chang, a 13-year-old seventh grader, developed a low-cost solar panel tracker using water and gravity to improve energy capture. The device, costing less than $25, tilts a solar panel without sensors or motors by filling a bucket with water, which shifts the panel's position as the sun moves. Outdoor tests showed it generated about 20% more voltage than fixed panels, though energy output gains require further analysis. Chang spent over a year refining the design with recycled materials. While commercial solar trackers exist, they are more expensive and complex. Rooftop installations face challenges due to wind and weather, making moving panels impractical for many. Chang’s invention offers a DIY alternative but has limitations, such as winter ice buildup. He is among 55 National STEM Champions recognized in 2026.

item.title: Developer creates bootable ZIP file as operating system
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Developer creates a 100% valid ZIP file that doubles as a BIOS-bootable operating system
Developer David Oberhollenzer, known as Goliath, created a ZIP file that functions as both a standard archive and a BIOS-bootable operating system. The ZIP file contains a Multiboot-compatible image, with the first file, ZIPHEAD.COM, housing boot code and necessary metadata. Goliath explained it was 'easy' to make the ZIP a valid Multiboot image by embedding the required 0x1BADB002 signature and bootloader instructions within the file's uncompressed data. BIOS compatibility was achieved by placing the 0x55AA boot signature at position 510 of the ZIP, ensuring it remains a valid archive while booting from floppy or standard PC BIOS. The file's structure leverages ZIP's unique metadata placement, with the first four bytes containing harmless CPU instructions and modified metadata acting as boot code. The project demonstrates how file formats can be repurposed for unconventional computing tasks.

item.title: Apple Develops iPhone Duo 2 with Face ID, but Launch Uncertain
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends Original headline: iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with Face ID are apparently ready at Apple, but the market might have to wait
Apple has developed prototypes of the iPhone Duo 2 with Face ID, according to Bloomberg. The first-generation iPhone Duo lacked facial recognition, using a side-mounted fingerprint sensor instead, which drew criticism. Engineers are working to integrate Face ID into the second-generation model's outer display, but its inclusion in the final product remains uncertain. The iPhone Duo 2, code-named V78, is expected to launch next fall, requiring hardware features to be finalized now. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman describes the Face ID integration as a toss-up, though not ruled out. Apple also plans to add an Action button, possibly combining it with the Camera Control button, and includes a telephoto zoom camera, thinner design, and lighter build for future foldable models. The company prioritizes facial recognition for its next foldable phone despite development challenges.

item.title: FBI Seizes Cloud Infrastructure in North Korea Cyberattack
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: FBI disrupts North Korean FaceStealer campaign behind $5 billion Binance hack
FBI and U.S. Department of Justice disrupted a North Korean cyber campaign named FaceStealer, linked to a $5 billion Binance hack. The operation involved seizing cloud infrastructure containing 900 victim videos. FaceStealer uses AI deepfakes, spear-phishing, and social engineering to steal cryptocurrency, with North Korea allegedly funding its government through these attacks. The campaign, active for at least 18 months, also targeted open-source software like JavaScript/NPM modules and Rust crates. A March 2026 incident compromised Axios, a widely used library, through a fake hiring scam. Attackers mimic legitimate companies, use deepfaked meetings, and deploy malware via 'technical problems' to steal credentials and access cryptocurrency wallets. The FBI warns of multi-stage attacks, using stolen data to target high-value victims like Binance developers. The campaign has siphoned about $400 million in cryptocurrency, with most of the Binance funds frozen or recovered.

item.title: HPE Juniper Routers Cause Nationwide Flight Ground Stop
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware Original headline: Two HPE Juniper network routers grounded all US flights on Friday
The FAA grounded all U.S. flights on Friday after newly installed Juniper routers, built by HPE Enterprise, overwhelmed the agency’s outdated copper communications network. The routers, part of an ongoing fiber upgrade, began broadcasting excessive data across the FAA’s system, causing communication failures between air traffic control and pilots. The issue first emerged at Indianapolis Center, prompting a nationwide search that identified two problematic routers in Arkansas and Texas. FAA technology chief Rebecca Guy noted the routers sent 1,000 connections every four to five seconds, far exceeding the capacity of the aging network. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford questioned whether the routers were faulty or poorly configured. The agency eventually disabled a specific router feature, restoring normal operations after four hours. The incident disrupted thousands of flights, with airlines estimating recovery could take days, similar to the 2024 CrowdStrike crash. HPE stated the routers functioned as intended, but the FAA continues investigating the cause.
